subject: Transit corridor recommendation for on-prem LLM access
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>
To: John Patel <john.patel@acme-med.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwoodinference.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Sun, 7 Mar 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Transit corridor recommendation for on-prem LLM access

Hi John,

Thanks again for the time earlier — good context on the workflow and compliance constraints. Attached is a short one-pager that summarizes three approaches we commonly evaluate for Redwood Private connectivity: (1) VPC peering / direct cloud interconnect, (2) PrivateLink / interface endpoint, and (3) site-to-site IPSec VPN.

High-level observations tailored to Acme's notes:
- VPC peering (or DirectConnect/ExpressRoute equivalent) gives full L3 reachability and predictable latency for high-throughput, multi-service integrations, but it typically requires cloud account-level peering and your networking team to accept a routed link.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is great when customers want strict surface-area reduction: only the Redwood service IPs are visible and you avoid broad VPC routing. It is operationally simpler for cross-account access but limits L3-level visibility and requires endpoint deployment in each AZ/region you use.
- Site-to-site IPSec VPN is the lowest-friction option when peering or PrivateLink are blocked by governance. It preserves encrypted transport and can be combined with a transit/routing appliance to offer stable egress IPs, but it adds NAT/MTU considerations and can increase operational burden for large-scale traffic.

Ask: can you confirm the following so we can recommend a single path?
1) Must traffic avoid public internet egress at all times (i.e., no NAT through internet-facing VPNs)?
2) Approx. RPS/requests per second and token/sec expectations for the pilot and steady-state.
3) Whether Acme requires static source IP(s) for allowlists (and if so, how many).
4) Any constraints on MTU / fragmentation (some regulated appliances require jumbo MTU disabled).

If peering is an option, we can propose a DirectConnect + TransitGateway design. If governance blocks peering, a combination of management-plane PrivateLink + data-plane IPSec to a transit gateway usually hits both compliance and operational goals.

I've attached the one-pager and a starter MAP template. If you can share a copy of your network topology PDF, we'll annotate it with the recommended handoff.

Next steps: once you confirm the bullets above, we can schedule a short architecture review with your network team (30–45m).

Cheers,

Mina Haddad
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Mina — thanks for the crisp writeup. A few clarifications from our side (answers inline):

> 1) Must traffic avoid public internet egress at all times?
Yes, for PHI-related calls we cannot traverse the public internet egress. We need either an on-prem link into our privately peered VPC or an IPsec to our edge that terminates into our private backbone.

> 2) Approx RPS/token expectations
Pilot: ~50 requests/sec (average), peak ~150 rps. Steady-state for our first production workload: 500–800 rps. Token rates will vary but assume medium-length responses.

> 3) Static source IP(s) for allowlists
We prefer a small set of static egress IPs (<= 4) for firewall rules.

> 4) MTU constraints
Our edge appliances prefer standard 1500 (no jumbo).

Also: we cannot do cross-account peering at the moment due to our cloud governance policy (security wants logical isolation by account). We do support DirectConnect to our transit appliance, and we can terminate IPsec on-prem.

I've attached our network topology (acme-network-topology-v2.pdf) and looped in netops. Look forward to the annotated version.

—John

Subject: Re: Transit corridor recommendation for on-prem LLM access

Mina / Connor — thanks, John for the topology. Quoting John's constraints above.

Recommendation (technical summary):
1) Primary: Site-to-site IPSec VPN to a Redwood-managed Transit Gateway (BGPod or TGW depending on cloud), with static source NAT performed at the transit layer to present up to 4 static egress IPs back to Acme for allowlisting. This meets the requirement to avoid public internet egress (traffic stays over IPsec into the transit) and respects Acme's no-peering policy.

Tradeoffs:
- Latency: slightly higher than DirectConnect/peering but within acceptable bounds for inference if we size appropriately and colocate endpoints in the same region. Expect +5–15ms typical additional latency vs peering depending on the transit path.
- Throughput & scale: IPsec tunnels are fine for pilot (50–150rps) but for sustained 500–800rps we recommend two tunnels (active/standby) with a managed egress appliance (or aggregate several tunnels to a transit). We'll need to bench throughput per cipher suite — AES-GCM helps.
- MTU/NAT: need to ensure DF handling and lower PMTU; we'll recommend MSS clamp to avoid fragmentation.
- Observability: VPN-only approaches require additional NAT/source tagging to preserve request traceability; we'll instrument token-level metadata in application headers and correlate with flow logs.

Optional: Management-plane PrivateLink for control traffic (healthchecks, admin APIs). That gives you an endpoint with minimal surface area for control while the data-plane runs over the IPSec transit. It adds a small amount of configuration but reduces broad routing exposure.

Operational asks for MAP and cutover:
- Provide preferred maintenance window for tunnel setup (2–4 hours).
- Provide contact for STA (who will accept BGP sessions if we bring Transit GW).
- Confirm firewall rules and target egress IPs are ok to be added in advance (we can reserve placeholders).

Connor / Mina — I'll draft a short design doc and a minimal runbook (BGP session params, PSK or certificate plan, MTU recommendation, perf bench steps). John — after we agree on the approach we can schedule a 45m architecture call to walk the runbook and test plan.

-kim
